name: Direct register access (BSRR) in bare-metal C, Packt Bare-Metal-Embedded-C-Programming companion code
baseline: STM32 HAL GPIO driver call HAL_GPIO_WritePin
workload: Third-party oscilloscope measurement of a PC8 set-then-reset loop on an STM32F072 Discovery (Cortex-M0, 48 MHz): two HAL_GPIO_WritePin calls versus two direct GPIOC->BSRR writes, pulse width read at four optimization levels.
claimed_speedup: BSRR register writes give a shorter pulse than HAL_GPIO_WritePin: 40.80 ns vs 396.0 ns at -O2 and -O3 (9.7x), 61.60 ns vs 418.0 ns at -O1 (6.8x), 61.60 ns vs 896.0 ns at -O0 (14.5x); ratios as printed in the benchmark README table. The book itself gives no timing, only qualitative text and a code-size comparison.
compiler_and_flags: Keil uVision5 with Arm Compiler 6 (AC6), -O0, -O1, -O2 and -O3 compared; other flags not stated (benchmark repo, not the book)
hardware: STM32F072RBT6 (Arm Cortex-M0) on 32F072BDISCOVERY, HCLK 48 MHz from HSE through PLL, 1 flash wait state, PC8 set to high speed; OWON SDS210S oscilloscope (100 MHz, 1 GS/s)
tradeoffs: Direct register writes tie the code to one MCU family and its reference manual, skip the HAL parameter checks and state handling (no error reporting, no clock enabling, no init helpers) and are harder to port than HAL or LL calls. The book's own chapters (Chapter3, Chapter6, Chapter7 and later) are register-level for GPIO, timers, ADC, UART, SPI, I2C, DMA, with its own linker script, startup file and CMSIS headers.
caveats: The numbers are NOT from the book or its repo: the book measures no time (only code size of the same GPIO setup in HAL, LL, C and assembly on STM32F411 at -O0, not in the repo). They come from an unrelated student repo (dotsolvit/stm32f0-gpio-speed-comparison, 0 stars, no license shown on the page, last commit 2026-09-24) measuring the same technique on a different chip (STM32F072 Cortex-M0, not the book's STM32F411 Cortex-M4). Its main.c loop confirms the code (HAL_GPIO_WritePin(GPIOC, GPIO_PIN_8, ...) versus GPIOC->BSRR = GPIO_BSRR_BS_8 / GPIO_BSRR_BR_8) and its method meets tier A, so the tier is capped at B because it measures another project's code on another chip. The measured pulse width is a toggle-loop artifact: at -O2 and -O3 the BSRR pulse train is non-uniform (grouped pulses, gap every 4 cycles, author attributes it to loop unrolling and flash prefetch, unverified) and ringing is visible below 100 ns. The loop only measures two GPIO writes, not a realistic firmware workload. The book repo's own GPIO driver (Chapter7-GpioInput/Src/gpio.c) writes GPIOA->BSRR |= LED_BS5, a read-modify-write form, not the plain store that was benchmarked. A second independent data point from a tutorial page (VictorTagayun/Basic_DSMPS_Tutorial, NUCLEO-F334R8 at 72 MHz, optimization level not stated): HAL_GPIO_WritePin loop 806 kHz versus GPIOC->BSRR/BRR 2.94 MHz toggle frequency. LL is not compared in either source. Chapter 2 and 6 comparison code (HAL, LL, C, assembly) is not visible in the repo folder listings I opened (Chapter1, Chapter2, Chapter7).
found_via: seed-record pass from https://github.com/PacktPublishing/Bare-Metal-Embedded-C-Programming; third-party timing found by WebSearch 'STM32 HAL versus LL versus register benchmark GPIO toggle cycles results README' which surfaced https://github.com/dotsolvit/stm32f0-gpio-speed-comparison

name: SizeBasedArena<T,N> bump arena (Orc Tribe), Packt C++ Memory Management companion code
baseline: glibc/libstdc++ operator new and operator delete (malloc/free)
workload: Book benchmark: allocate then destroy 1,000,000 16-byte Orc objects with class-specific operator new/delete backed by a mutex-guarded bump arena, single thread, std::chrono timing in microseconds, one run.
claimed_speedup: operator new: 23433 us standard library vs 17906 us Meyers-singleton arena vs 17573 us global-singleton arena (arena about 76.4% of the standard time); operator delete: 7943 us standard vs 638 us Meyers-singleton arena (8.03%) vs 0 us global-singleton arena (no-op). Numbers are the book's printed figures as relayed in the seed lead; they are not printed anywhere in the repo.
compiler_and_flags: Book: online gcc 15 at -O2 (per the seed lead; not in the repo, whose files only carry wandbox permalinks that I could not open: wandbox.org ENOTFOUND). libstdc++ inferred from gcc.
tradeoffs: Bump allocation only: freed memory is never reused, delete is a no-op, so memory is reclaimed only when the arena is destroyed. Capacity N*sizeof(T) is malloc'd up front, with no bounds check on exhaustion. A mutex is taken on every allocation. Serves one class (operator new/delete overloads for Orc); operator new[] and delete[] assert false. A SizeBasedArena-safer variant adds static_assert(std::is_final_v<T>) so derived classes cannot be allocated from a too-small slot.
caveats: First-party book measurement: one run on an unnamed online gcc 15 machine, CPU not stated, flags and numbers come from the book, not the repo. The repo does carry the benchmark programs in chapter10 (carnage-stdlib-version.cpp, carnage-homemade-version-meyers-singleton.cpp, carnage-homemade-version-global-singleton.cpp, carnage-homemade-version-SizeBasedArena.cpp, carnage-homemade-version-SizeBasedArena-safer.cpp) with no printed results or build lines. Not like for like: the arena never reuses memory, delete does nothing (0 us in the global-singleton version), and the test is allocate-all then free-all, the best case for a bump allocator. In the Meyers-singleton version the arena's one-time malloc of 1,000,000 Orc slots runs inside the first timed operator new call. Generic typed-arena speedup over malloc is well known; the evidence is a teaching example.
found_via: seed-record pass from https://github.com/packtpublishing/c-plus-plus-memory-management (chapter10 folder listing and source files opened via raw.githubusercontent.com)

name: ChunkSizedAllocator<N,Sz...> chunked fixed-size-class pool, Packt C++ Memory Management companion code
baseline: glibc/libstdc++ operator new and operator delete (malloc/free)
workload: Book benchmark: 300,000 allocations (100,000 each of 30-, 60- and 100-byte objects) through placement-style operator new(ChunkSizedAllocator&), then destroy and deallocate through std::function, microseconds, one run.
claimed_speedup: Chunked version 12,032 us versus 13,360 us for the standard operator new/delete version, about 90.05% of the standard time (roughly 1.1x, derived from the book's two figures). Numbers are the book's printed figures as relayed in the seed lead; not printed in the repo.
compiler_and_flags: Book: online gcc 15 at -O2 (per the seed lead; not in the repo, which only links a wandbox permalink I could not open). libstdc++ inferred from gcc.
tradeoffs: Fixed pools: N blocks per size class (rounded up to powers of two) allocated up front with malloc, allocation falls back to ::operator new when a pool is exhausted or the size does not fit. Freed memory is never reused (deallocate only checks whether the pointer lies in a pool). Deallocation does a linear scan over the size classes. A mutex guards allocate; the lock in deallocate is commented out. new[] and delete[] are left as an exercise.
caveats: First-party book measurement: one run, online gcc 15 at -O2, CPU not stated; the gain is small (about 10%). The upfront pool allocation in the constructor is outside the timed region. Both sides pay std::function type erasure and a std::vector of 300,000 pairs. The book itself warns that locking the mutex strongly affects the gain and locking in deallocate would likely erase it. No memory reuse, so not like for like with a real allocator. Benchmark program is chapter10/chunk_sized_allocator.cpp (opened via raw.githubusercontent.com): it prints the two timings but the repo holds no results, compiler line or CPU.

name: STM32 Low Layer (LL) driver library
workload: Third-party GPIO pin toggle loop on a NUCLEO-F334R8 (72 MHz): HAL_GPIO_WritePin set/reset versus LL_GPIO_SetOutputPin/LL_GPIO_ResetOutputPin versus HAL_GPIO_TogglePin versus LL_GPIO_TogglePin versus direct GPIOC->BSRR/BRR, measured toggle frequency on PC9.
claimed_speedup: LL_GPIO_SetOutputPin/ResetOutputPin 1.09 MHz vs HAL_GPIO_WritePin set/reset 806 kHz (about 1.35x, derived from page data); HAL_GPIO_TogglePin and LL_GPIO_TogglePin both 625 kHz (no gain); direct GPIOC->BSRR/BRR 2.94 MHz.
hardware: NUCLEO-F334R8 (STM32F334R8, Cortex-M4), 8 MHz external input with PLLMUL 9, system clock up to 72 MHz
stars_or_usage: 209 stars (STM32F4 HAL/LL driver repository); shipped beside HAL in the STM32Cube MCU packages
tradeoffs: LL is closer to the registers than HAL: no handle structures, no state machine, little or no parameter validation and no timeout or error handling in the register-level calls, so peripheral setup order, clock enabling and error paths are the caller's job. LL is not offered for every peripheral (ST's driver manuals reportedly say it is not provided where optimized access is not a key feature, USB for example; search snippet only) and code is less portable across STM32 families than HAL.
caveats: The speed numbers are third-party, from a different family (STM32F334, not the F4 driver repo this record points at; the LL API is shared across families) and from a tutorial page, not a controlled study. The compiler and optimization level are not stated: a linked repo (VictorTagayun/STM32F334_HAL_LL_REG_GPIO) holds the toggle main.c with each variant commented in or out and an .ioc file (STM32CubeIDE, HAL assert off, PA8 high speed), but its README has no results or flags. HAL overhead varies about 2x between -O0 and -O1 in another STM32F0 test, so a default Debug build could inflate the gap. The toggle-pin variants show no LL gain. ST's own claim (LL is leaner and faster than HAL) has no numbers on the F4 driver repository page I opened (no benchmark or footprint data seen; Release_Notes.html was not opened). Code-size evidence exists only as forum snippets that I could not open (community.st.com and eevblog.com are ENOTFOUND here): a post titled 'Is HAL driver Require more space compared to LL' reportedly shows a GPIO plus LPUART build of 10128 bytes with HAL versus 5848 bytes with LL, chip and flags unstated (snippet only), and an EEVblog comment reports about 6K to 2K for a basic build (snippet only).
found_via: seed-record pass from https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32f4xx_hal_driver; third-party timing found via WebSearch 'stm32 HAL versus LL performance test DWT cycle count results table' which surfaced https://github.com/VictorTagayun/Basic_DSMPS_Tutorial

name: AFL (american fuzzy lop)
baseline: blind fuzzing (random mutation without coverage guidance)
workload: Coverage reached on GNU patch 2.7.3 compiled with -O3, seeded with a dummy text file, one pass over the afl-fuzz input queue, AFL's coverage-guided model against blind fuzzing and against block-only and edge-only guidance; a second experiment with only deterministic stages seeded with a valid unified diff.
claimed_speedup: Coverage, not speed: AFL model reached 1,765 blocks and 2,597 edges versus 182 blocks / 205 edges (blind fuzzing S, single round) and 228 blocks / 265 edges (blind fuzzing L, comparable number of cycles), from an initial file at 156 / 163. Deterministic-only experiment: AFL model 1,452 blocks / 2,040 edges and 1 unique crash versus blind fuzzing 1,101 / 1,409 and 0 crashes. Separate speed claims in the same docs: LLVM-mode instrumentation up to around 2x faster for slow CPU-bound programs and within 10% for fast binaries (versus afl-gcc/afl-clang assembly-level rewriting); fork server 1.5x-2x; deferred fork server 10x+ on some targets. The README calls the fuzzer far superior to blind fuzzing or coverage-only tools.
compiler_and_flags: Target GNU patch 2.7.3 compiled with -O3; instrumenting compiler and afl-fuzz build flags not stated
stars_or_usage: 4.2k stars, 672 forks; repository archived by the owner on 2024-03-22
tradeoffs: Needs an instrumented target (afl-gcc, afl-clang or the LLVM plugin; QEMU mode for black-box binaries is about 2-5x slower than compile-time instrumentation) and takes input as a file; persistent and deferred modes need small code changes and care to reset state. Archived and read-only; the maintained community fork is AFL++ (not checked in this session).
caveats: First-party table in the project's own technical notes, one target and one session, no CPU, no run count and no repeat variance, so not reproducible as written. It measures discovered blocks and edges, not execs per second or time to bug, and the blind baseline is AFL's own fuzzer with guidance removed, not an independent blind fuzzer. The docs do not claim to beat libFuzzer: llvm_mode/README.llvm says the persistent mode is not as fast as pure in-process fuzzing such as LLVM's LibFuzzer, though much faster than the fork() model and more robust. No AFL versus libFuzzer numbers found in the repo. Last commit date taken from the github.com commits page; repo archived and read-only.
found_via: seed-record pass from https://github.com/google/AFL; numbers from docs/technical_details.txt, llvm_mode/README.llvm and docs/perf_tips.txt (opened via raw.githubusercontent.com)
